subtype: Minority view that turned out right [Observer]
passage:
Monday. In the launch meeting, Indu said the supplier’s delivery date was unrealistic. Eight of them nodded past her and moved on. Rekha thought Indu was being negative.
Twelve days later the supplier missed the date. The launch slipped, and the team sat in a quiet room. Someone said, “Indu did say.” Nobody answered.
The following Friday the manager thanked Indu in front of everyone. Rekha, at the back, felt an odd distance from herself. She had nodded with the rest. It struck her that being outnumbered had nothing to do with being wrong.

qa.q: What did Indu say in the launch meeting?
qa.a: Indu said the supplier's delivery date was unrealistic.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel at the back of the room when the manager thanked Indu?
qa.a: Rekha felt oddly detached and thoughtful, aware that she had nodded with the rest. The realisation that being outnumbered is not the same as being wrong shows in her reflection.

qa.q: What could the team do differently the next time someone raises a concern?
qa.a: They could ask the person to explain the reasons before moving on and note the concern in the plan. That would treat a lone warning as information.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt when everyone nodded past her, and again when the manager thanked her?
qa.a: Indu was probably frustrated and unheard in the meeting, and later validated but perhaps also uneasy that it took a missed date. The passage shows only what people said.

grounding: Shows an observer recalling a lone voice that warned of a problem the group dismissed, and that being outnumbered does not mean being wrong.

passage:
Salma, come here. I’m Kashish, and I’ll tell you about a lake picnic when I was twenty-two. Our college group had hired two boats, and someone had tied up the smaller one for the second load.
Meena, a quiet girl from our class, said, “That boat has a crack near the back.” Everyone laughed. “Always worrying,” they said.
Meena did not laugh back. She said again, calmly, “Please, look at it.” I looked, and I wanted to say she was right, but I stayed quiet.
Then the boatman checked, and the boat was not used. It leaked within minutes. Nobody said sorry to Meena, but they never called her a worrier again.

qa.q: How old was Kashish at the lake picnic?
How might Meena have felt when everyone laughed at her warning?
qa.a: Meena was probably embarrassed and worried, but she stayed calm and repeated it. Not laughing back shows she cared more about safety than the mocking.

qa.q: What choice did Meena make that turned out to matter?
qa.a: Meena repeated calmly, “Please, look at it,” instead of dropping the warning when laughed at. That got the boat checked before anyone used it.

qa.q: How might the boatman have felt about Meena's warning?
qa.a: The boatman probably took it seriously once it was raised, since the boat was checked and withdrawn. The passage shows only that action.

grounding: An elder recalls a lone voice warning of a cracked boat that the group laughed at and that turned out to be right.
